finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id performs the delete without enforcing the authorization check because authorize() is called without await, so any caller can delete any report.
finding.source: Any HTTP DELETE request to /reports/:id with an attacker-chosen id (server.js:18-19).

trace.note: DELETE handler receives req.params.id
db.reports.get loads the report
authorize(req.user, 'delete', report) is invoked without await; returns a promise that is discarded
db.reports.remove runs before the grants lookup resolves
responds 204 regardless of the authorization outcome
grants lookup; a failed check throws 403 only inside the unawaited promise, which nothing catches

finding.guards_checked: Grant check in authorize() (server.js:9-16) is correct when awaited and fails closed. It is not enforced on this route because of the missing await. The PUT route does await it (server.js:27), so the defect is specific to DELETE. No middleware or route-level authorization observed in this file.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. The only check is authorize() at server.js:9-16, which throws on failure, but it is called without await at server.js:20, so its rejection never reaches the handler. Nothing between the request and db.reports.remove at server.js:21 blocks the delete. The only auth-like call is the session copy at server.js:4-7, which does not check permissions. The PUT route at server.js:27 awaits the check, so the gap is specific to DELETE.
verdict.reason: At server.js:20 authorize() is not awaited, so the db.reports.remove call at server.js:21 runs and the 204 at server.js:22 is sent whether or not the grant check at server.js:11-14 fails. The attacker only needs an authenticated session (req.session.user, server.js:5), so any logged-in low-privilege user can delete any report. The session setup is not in this file, so I could not confirm how sessions are issued.

finding.claim: Unhandled promise rejections from authorize() and from async handlers can crash the Node process, allowing a single crafted request to cause denial of service.
finding.source: Unauthenticated or unprivileged request to /reports/<id>, including a nonexistent id or a request without req.user (server.js:5, 19, 26).
finding.sink: Unhandled promise rejection; Node's default unhandled-rejections=throw terminates the process on Node 15+.

trace.note: req.user is copied from req.session.user without a presence check
db.reports.get may return null for an unknown id
authorize() dereferences user.id and resource.id, throwing a TypeError on null or undefined inputs
DELETE: the rejection from authorize() is unhandled because the call is not awaited
PUT: the awaited rejection propagates into an async Express 4 handler with no catch, so it is unhandled

finding.guards_checked: No try/catch, no Express error handler, no null check on report or req.user, no process-level unhandledRejection handler in this file. Crash behavior is reasoned from Node's documented default, not reproduced; actual impact depends on the Node version and on whether db.reports.get returns null or throws for unknown ids.

verdict.guard_found: none. No try/catch around the async handlers or the authorize() call, no Express error handler, and no process.on("unhandledRejection") in server.js. server.js:20 calls authorize() without await or .catch, so its rejection is unhandled. server.js:27 awaits authorize() inside an Express 4 async handler with no catch. Nothing in this file blocks the 403 or TypeError rejections.
verdict.reason: The DELETE path at server.js:20 drops the promise from authorize() (defined at server.js:9-16), so any rejection there is unhandled, and the PUT path at server.js:27 has the same problem. Any authenticated user without a delete grant on an existing report (server.js:20, which throws the 403 at line 14), or any request that yields a null report (server.js:19) or a missing req.user (server.js:5), produces an unhandled rejection that Node 15+ turns into a process exit by default. The trace cites line 9 for the dereference, but the dereference is on line 10 (db.grants(user.id, resource.id)); that is a line-number nit and does not change the result. Caveat: session middleware is not in this file, so whether req.user is ever missing depends on code I could not see, and a process-level handler elsewhere would change the impact. The attacker needs only a session, not admin rights. The 403 case does not need a null report or a missing user.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire request body to the database update, so a caller with write permission can set arbitrary fields such as owner, id, or access columns (mass assignment).

trace.note: express.json() parses the request body into req.body
PUT handler loads the report
write grant is checked and awaited correctly
entire req.body is passed to db.reports.update with no field allowlist

finding.guards_checked: Write-grant check at server.js:27. No schema validation, no field allowlist, no removal of id, owner, or grant fields. The db.reports.update implementation is not in this directory, so the reachable columns are unverified.

verdict.guard_found: Write-grant check at server.js:27 (`await authorize(req.user, "write", report)`). It throws a 403 on failure and the await is correct, so only callers holding the "write" grant on this report reach line 28. No field allowlist, schema validation, or stripping of id/owner/grant fields exists between server.js:28 and the sink.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (server.js:3, 26, 27, 28), and the write-grant check at server.js:27 is awaited and throws, so it limits the caller to write-granted users, but nothing at server.js:28 restricts which fields of req.body reach db.reports.update, so any write-granted user can pass fields such as owner or access columns. The specific columns that are actually writable depend on db.reports.update, which is not in this directory, so the severity is unverified even though the unguarded mass assignment is confirmed.

finding.claim: The file has no authentication gate: req.session is read without a presence check and req.user is never verified, so enforcement depends entirely on session middleware that is not in this directory.
finding.source: Any HTTP request to the app (server.js:4-5).
finding.sink: req.user assignment at server.js:5, consumed by authorize() at server.js:10 and the route handlers.

trace.note: req.user = req.session.user; throws if req.session is undefined
authorize() reads user.id; undefined user leads to TypeError
app.listen(3003) binds without any auth middleware on routes

finding.guards_checked: None in this file. Session creation and login enforcement would have to live in code outside this directory.

verdict.guard_found: None in server.js. Line 5 has no session check, but the missing gate is not an exploit by itself: with no session middleware in this directory, req.session is undefined and every request throws a TypeError at server.js:5, so the app fails closed. The trace's line 9 is the authorize() signature; the user.id read is at server.js:10, so the trace is misdescribed.
verdict.reason: The trace cites server.js:9 for the user.id read, but that read is at server.js:10, and in this file req.session is never set (server.js:5), so every request crashes at server.js:5 rather than reaching authorize(). The real defect in this file is different: the DELETE handler calls authorize() without await at server.js:20, so the grant check's rejection is never seen and the delete at server.js:21 runs for any user, which is a separate finding that this candidate does not describe.

finding.claim: The raw req.params.id string is passed to db.reports.get without validation, which may enable SQL or NoSQL injection if the db layer concatenates it into a query. Unverified.
finding.source: req.params.id from the URL path of DELETE and PUT /reports/:id (server.js:19, 26).

trace.note: req.params.id passed unvalidated to db.reports.get
same unvalidated pattern on PUT

finding.guards_checked: No type or format validation on the id. The db module is not defined or required in this directory, so the query construction cannot be checked.

verdict.guard_found: none. server.js:19 and server.js:26 pass req.params.id straight to db.reports.get with no type, format, or allowlist check, and nothing in the directory parameterizes or escapes it. The db module is absent, so whether it reaches a query unsafely cannot be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace lines match the claim (server.js:19 and :26 pass the unvalidated req.params.id to db.reports.get), but the injection sink lives in a db module that is not in the directory, so whether it concatenates the id into a query cannot be decided from this code. The app also does not show how an attacker would obtain a session (req.session.user at server.js:5 has no visible session setup), so reachability is unknown too.
